name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CLASS_11_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MATCH_Q01 - Definitions and mathematical forms of kinematic quantities

questiontext.text:
Match Column I (Physical Quantity) with Column II (Mathematical Definition):

Column I (Physical Quantity) Column II (Mathematical Definition)
(A) Instantaneous velocity(I) \(\lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}\)
(B) Average velocity(II) \(x(t_2) - x(t_1)\)
(C) Instantaneous acceleration(III) \(\lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\)
(D) Displacement(IV) \(\frac{x(t_2) - x(t_1)}{t_2 - t_1}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In kinematics along a straight coordinate axis, each physical quantity possesses a rigorous mathematical definition in terms of position coordinate \(x(t)\), velocity \(v(t)\), and time \(t\).

Step 2: Evaluation of Instantaneous Velocity
Instantaneous velocity is the time rate of change of position at a specific instant, defined as the differential limit \(v = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\). This pairs instantaneous velocity with the differential limit of position.

Step 3: Evaluation of Average Velocity
Average velocity over a time interval from \(t_1\) to \(t_2\) is the net displacement divided by the elapsed time, \(\bar{v} = \frac{x(t_2) - x(t_1)}{t_2 - t_1}\). This pairs average velocity with the quotient of total position change over elapsed time.

Step 4: Evaluation of Instantaneous Acceleration
Instantaneous acceleration is the time rate of change of velocity at an instant, defined as \(a = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}\). This pairs instantaneous acceleration with the differential limit of velocity.

Step 5: Evaluation of Displacement and Final Conclusion
Displacement is the change in the position coordinate of the particle between initial and final instants, \(\Delta x = x(t_2) - x(t_1)\). Combining all four pairings yields the complete set: instantaneous velocity pairs with the differential limit of position, average velocity pairs with the ratio of position difference to time difference, instantaneous acceleration pairs with the differential limit of velocity, and displacement pairs with the difference between final and initial coordinates. This corresponds to A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CLASS_11_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MATCH_Q02 - Interpretation of slopes and areas of graphs

questiontext.text:
Match Column I (Graphical Feature) with Column II (Physical Meaning):

Column I (Graphical Feature) Column II (Physical Meaning)
(A) Slope of the tangent to position–time curve(I) Motion with positive acceleration
(B) Area bounded under velocity–time curve and time axis(II) Instantaneous acceleration
(C) Slope of the tangent to velocity–time curve(III) Displacement over the time interval
(D) Upward-bending curvature on position–time curve(IV) Instantaneous velocity

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Kinematic graphs visually encapsulate the calculus relationships between position \(x\), velocity \(v = \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\), and acceleration \(a = \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 x}{\mathrm{d}t^2}\). Derivatives correspond to slopes of tangents, definite integrals correspond to enclosed areas, and second derivatives determine concavity.

Step 2: Evaluation of Position–Time Slope
The derivative \(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\) is geometrically represented by the slope of the tangent to the position–time curve, giving the instantaneous velocity. Thus, the slope of the position–time curve pairs with instantaneous velocity.

Step 3: Evaluation of Velocity–Time Area
The definite integral \(\int_{t_1}^{t_2} v(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\) geometrically corresponds to the area enclosed between the velocity–time curve and the time axis, representing the net displacement. Thus, the area under the velocity–time curve pairs with displacement over the time interval.

Step 4: Evaluation of Velocity–Time Slope
The derivative \(\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}\) is geometrically represented by the slope of the tangent to the velocity–time curve, giving the instantaneous acceleration. Thus, the slope of the velocity–time curve pairs with instantaneous acceleration.

Step 5: Evaluation of Curvature and Final Conclusion
The second derivative \(\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 x}{\mathrm{d}t^2}\) determines the concavity of the position–time curve: a curve that is concave upward (curves upward) signifies \(\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 x}{\mathrm{d}t^2} > 0\), which corresponds to positive acceleration. Combining all four pairs yields: position–time slope matches instantaneous velocity, velocity–time area matches displacement, velocity–time slope matches instantaneous acceleration, and upward curvature matches positive acceleration. This corresponds to A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CLASS_11_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MATCH_Q03 - Kinematic parameters and analytical mathematical formulas

questiontext.text:
Match Column I (Kinematic Parameter) with Column II (Analytical Expression):

Column I (Kinematic Parameter) Column II (Analytical Expression)
(A) Stopping distance under uniform braking retardation \(a\)(I) \(\sqrt{2gh}\)
(B) Distance traversed in the \(n^{\text{th}}\) second under uniform gravity from rest(II) \(\frac{v_0^2}{2a}\)
(C) Speed acquired falling freely through height \(h\) from rest(III) \(v_0 t_r\)
(D) Distance traversed during reaction time \(t_r\) at constant speed \(v_0\)(IV) \(\frac{1}{2}g(2n - 1)\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Uniformly accelerated motion is governed by the kinematic equations \(v = v_0 + at\), \(x = v_0 t + \frac{1}{2}at^2\), and \(v^2 = v_0^2 + 2ax\). Specific physical boundary conditions yield characteristic expressions for stopping distance, nth-second displacement, free fall velocity, and reaction travel.

Step 2: Evaluation of Stopping Distance
For a vehicle brought to rest from initial speed \(v_0\) under constant deceleration \(a\), setting final speed \(v = 0\) in \(v^2 = v_0^2 - 2a d_s\) gives stopping distance \(d_s = \frac{v_0^2}{2a}\). Thus, stopping distance pairs with \(\frac{v_0^2}{2a}\).

Step 3: Evaluation of Distance in the nth Second
For an object released from rest (\(u = 0\)) under uniform gravitational acceleration \(g\), the distance covered in the \(n^{\text{th}}\) second is \(s_n = u + \frac{1}{2}g(2n - 1) = \frac{1}{2}g(2n - 1)\). Thus, distance in the nth second pairs with \(\frac{1}{2}g(2n - 1)\).

Step 4: Evaluation of Speed after Free Fall
For free fall from rest over height \(h\) under acceleration \(g\), using \(v^2 = 0 + 2gh\) yields final speed \(v = \sqrt{2gh}\). Thus, speed acquired falling through height \(h\) pairs with \(\sqrt{2gh}\).

Step 5: Evaluation of Reaction Distance and Final Conclusion
During the driver's reaction time \(t_r\), the brakes have not yet taken effect, so the car moves at constant initial speed \(v_0\). The distance traveled is \(d = v_0 t_r\). Thus, reaction distance pairs with \(v_0 t_r\). Combining all four pairs yields: stopping distance pairs with \(\frac{v_0^2}{2a}\), distance in the nth second pairs with \(\frac{1}{2}g(2n - 1)\), speed acquired in free fall pairs with \(\sqrt{2gh}\), and reaction distance pairs with \(v_0 t_r\). This corresponds to A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CLASS_11_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MATCH_Q04 - Motion characteristics matched to velocity time profiles

questiontext.text:
Match Column I (Physical Motion Description) with Column II (Velocity–Time Graph Characteristics):

Column I (Physical Motion Description) Column II (Velocity–Time Graph Characteristics)
(A) Motion in positive direction with uniform positive acceleration(I) Straight line with negative slope intersecting the time axis to enter the negative velocity region
(B) Motion in positive direction with uniform negative acceleration reversing direction(II) Straight line parallel to the time axis with zero slope
(C) Free fall from rest in negative direction under constant downward gravity(III) Straight line starting at positive initial velocity with positive slope rising upward
(D) Rectilinear motion with uniform velocity and zero acceleration(IV) Straight line starting from the origin with constant negative slope descending into negative velocities

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Consider rectilinear motion described by velocity \(v(t) = v_0 + at\). On a \(v\)–\(t\) Cartesian plot, the initial velocity \(v_0\) represents the vertical intercept at \(t = 0\), and the acceleration \(a\) represents the constant slope \(\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}\).

Step 2: Evaluation of Positive Direction with Positive Acceleration
Here, initial velocity is positive (\(v_0 > 0\)) and acceleration is positive (\(a > 0\)). The \(v\)–\(t\) curve begins on the positive vertical axis and slopes upward with positive slope, representing a straight line starting at positive velocity and rising upward. Thus, this motion pairs with the rising straight line with positive slope.

Step 3: Evaluation of Positive Motion Reversing under Negative Acceleration
Here, the initial velocity is positive (\(v_0 > 0\)) but acceleration is negative (\(a < 0\)). The velocity decreases linearly, passes through zero when the particle momentarily turns back at the time axis, and continues downward into negative velocity values. Thus, this motion pairs with the straight line with negative slope that intersects the time axis to enter negative velocities.

Step 4: Evaluation of Free Fall from Rest in Negative Direction
Choosing the upward direction as positive, a body dropped from rest has \(v_0 = 0\) and constant downward acceleration \(a = -g\). The velocity is given by \(v(t) = -gt\), which starts at the origin and slopes downward linearly into the negative velocity region. Thus, this motion pairs with the straight line starting from the origin with constant negative slope.

Step 5: Evaluation of Zero Acceleration and Final Conclusion
When acceleration is zero (\(a = 0\)), the velocity is constant: \(v(t) = u\). The rate of change \(\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} = 0\), producing a horizontal straight line parallel to the time axis. Thus, zero acceleration pairs with the line parallel to the time axis. Combining all four pairs yields: positive motion with positive acceleration pairs with the rising positive-slope line, reversal under negative acceleration pairs with the line crossing the time axis, free fall from rest pairs with the line descending from the origin into negative values, and uniform velocity pairs with the line parallel to the time axis. This corresponds to A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.
